Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Treat $(t,x)$ as the parameter block and $z$ as the unknown block in [F2]. Its hypotheses hold because $g$ is $C^k$, $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, and $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. Therefore [F2] gives neighborhoods $U,V$ and a unique $C^k$ function $\psi$ with the stated equivalence and derivative formula. Splitting that combined derivative into its $t$ and $x$ blocks gives the two displayed identities.

Differentiating $g(t,x,\psi(t,x))=0$ in the $t$ direction using [F3] gives $g_t+g_z\psi_t=0$; multiplying by $g_z^{-1}$ gives $\psi_t=-g_z^{-1}g_t$. Differentiating in each $x$ direction gives $g_x+g_z\psi_x=0$, hence $\psi_x=-g_z^{-1}g_x$.

The map $(t,x)\mapsto (t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$, so [F3] applied to its composition with the $C^k$ map $f$ shows $F(t,x)=f(t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$. On the selected chart the equivalence in step 1.1 forces every DAE solution to have $z(t)=\psi(t,x(t))$, and substitution gives $x'=F(t,x)$; conversely, a reduced solution paired with $z=\psi(t,x)$ satisfies both DAE equations.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$, $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^k$ for $k\ge1$. Suppose $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$ and $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. Then there are neighborhoods $U$ of $(t_*,x_*)$ and $V$ of $z_*$, and a unique $C^k$ map $\psi:U\to V$, such that, for $(t,x)\in U$ and $z\in V$,

$$
g(t,x,z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\psi(t,x).
$$

Its derivatives satisfy

$$
\psi_t=-g_z^{-1}g_t,\qquad \psi_x=-g_z^{-1}g_x,
$$

with the derivatives of $g$ evaluated at $(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. The reduced vector field $F(t,x)=f(t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$ on $U$. Thus solutions of the DAE that stay in this selected chart are exactly solutions of $x'=F(t,x)$ paired with $z=\psi(t,x)$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Fix any $(t,x)\in K$, put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$, and set $\delta=z-z_*$. The branch has $m\ge1$ algebraic variables. Since $g(t,x,z_*)=0$, apply [F2] on $s\in[0,1]$ to the $C^1$ path $g(t,x,z_*+s\delta)$, whose segment stays in the branch ball. It gives $g(t,x,z)=G_*(t,x)\delta+R$, where $R=\int_0^1(g_z(t,x,z_*+s\delta)-G_*(t,x))\delta\,ds$. The anchored Jacobian bound and integral norm inequality give $\|R\|_2\le\int_0^1\Lambda s\|\delta\|_2^2\,ds=(\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2^2\le(\sqrt m\,\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$.

The common lower singular-value bound gives $\|G_*(t,x)\delta\|_2\ge\gamma\|\delta\|_2$. Using [F3] in the form $\|G_*(t,x)\delta+R\|_2\ge\|G_*(t,x)\delta\|_2-\|R\|_2$, we obtain $\|g(t,x,z)\|_2\ge(\gamma-(\sqrt m\,\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2)\|\delta\|_2$. If $\Lambda>0$, $\|\delta\|_2<\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$ makes the parenthesis at least $\gamma/2$; if $\Lambda=0$, it equals $\gamma$. In either case it is at least $\gamma/2$, with the same constants for every $(t,x)\in K$.
Dividing the inequality in step 2.1 by $\gamma/2>0$ proves the asserted residual-to-state estimate for every candidate in the branch ball.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$, $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^k$ for $k\ge1$. Suppose $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$ and $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. Then there are neighborhoods $U$ of $(t_*,x_*)$ and $V$ of $z_*$, and a unique $C^k$ map $\psi:U\to V$, such that, for $(t,x)\in U$ and $z\in V$,

$$
g(t,x,z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\psi(t,x).
$$

Its derivatives satisfy

$$
\psi_t=-g_z^{-1}g_t,\qquad \psi_x=-g_z^{-1}g_x,
$$

with the derivatives of $g$ evaluated at $(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. The reduced vector field $F(t,x)=f(t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$ on $U$. Thus solutions of the DAE that stay in this selected chart are exactly solutions of $x'=F(t,x)$ paired with $z=\psi(t,x)$.

Let $K$ be a compact set of base points $(t,x)$ in a selected branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], and put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$. Suppose $g(t,x,\cdot)$ is $C^2$ on $B(z_*,\rho)$ for every $(t,x)\in K$. Let $G_*(t,x)=g_z(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. Assume common constants $\gamma>0$, $\Lambda\ge0$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy

$$
\|G_*(t,x)v\|_2\ge\gamma\|v\|_2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^m),\qquad \|g_z(t,x,z)-G_*(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Lambda\|z-\psi(t,x)\|_2
$$

for every $(t,x)\in K$ and $z\in B(\psi(t,x),\rho)$; if $\Lambda>0$, assume $\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$. Then, uniformly for all such base points and candidates,

$$
\|z-z_*\|_2\le \frac{2}{\gamma}\|g(t,x,z)\|_2.
$$

The estimate is local: it applies only to candidates in the specified branch ball and does not turn a residual into a global branch or uniqueness certificate.

Input $f,g$, a constant grid $t_n=t_0+nh$ with $h>0$ and $N_t\ge2$, two starting pairs $(X_0,Z_0),(X_1,Z_1)$, and a selected open tube $\mathcal T\subset\Omega$ inside the local branch chart of [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], where $g(t,x,z)=0$ is equivalent to $z=\psi(t,x)$. For each time $t$, write $\mathcal T_t=\{(X,Z):(t,X,Z)\in\mathcal T\}$ for the open state slice used as the Newton evaluation domain. Also input positive residual tolerances $\eta_d,\eta_a$, a finite Newton-correction budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and two starting algebraic-residual bounds $\eta_{a,0},\eta_{a,1}\ge0$. Return invalid-grid for a nonpositive step or fewer than two starting states, and invalid-input for incompatible dimensions, data outside the function domains, or $(X_j,Z_j)\notin\mathcal T_{t_j}$ for either $j=0,1$. Compute $r^a_j=g(t_j,X_j,Z_j)$ for both $j=0,1$; if $\|r^a_j\|_2>\eta_{a,j}$ for either start, return inconsistent-initial-data.

For $n=2,\ldots,N_t$, form

$$
R_n(X,Z)=\bigl(3X-4X_{n-1}+X_{n-2}-2h f(t_n,X,Z),\ g(t_n,X,Z)\bigr)
$$

and

$$
\mathcal R_n(X,Z)=\left(\frac{3X-4X_{n-1}+X_{n-2}-2h f(t_n,X,Z)}{2h\eta_d},\ \frac{g(t_n,X,Z)}{\eta_a}\right).
$$

Use $(2X_{n-1}-X_{n-2},Z_{n-1})$ as the Newton seed. Before calling Newton, if $(2X_{n-1}-X_{n-2},Z_{n-1})\notin\mathcal T_{t_n}$, return invalid-trial with the computed prefix. Otherwise call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on $\mathcal R_n$ with tolerance $1$, budget $B$, and $\mathcal T_{t_n}$ as the evaluation domain. Append a candidate only when Newton reports root and the candidate lies in $\mathcal T_{t_n}$; reevaluate $R_n$ once to record its unscaled residual blocks. Otherwise return the corresponding singular-Jacobian, invalid-trial, or iteration-budget-exhausted status with the computed prefix. The input functions are defined on the selected tube, so no separate evaluation-failure branch is needed. If all steps are accepted, return completed and the state sequence $((X_0,Z_0),\ldots,(X_{N_t},Z_{N_t}))$.

For an accepted step, the constant-step BDF2 derivative residual is
$$
r^d_n=\frac{3X_n-4X_{n-1}+X_{n-2}}{2h}-f(t_n,X_n,Z_n),
$$
and the algebraic residual is $r^a_n=g(t_n,X_n,Z_n)$.  The procedure makes no claim that Newton finds a root or that an accepted state is the exact selected branch root.

Use the coupled $(d+m)$-dimensional residual and its current block Jacobian. Record residual queries, Jacobian assemblies and correction solves separately; backend costs are not specified.

Input a vector field $f(t,y)$, a finite grid $t_0,\ldots,t_N$, starting states $Y_0,Y_1\in\mathbb R^d$ (so $N\ge1$), and for each later step a prescribed closed ball $B_{n+1}\subset\mathbb R^d$ that specifies the admissible implicit branch. Before any evaluation, if either starting state has dimension different from $d$, return `invalid-input`; otherwise, if any time increment is nonpositive, return `invalid-grid`. Set $h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$ and $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}$ for $1\le n<N$.

Also supply an exact branch oracle $\mathcal O$ for the step equations below. On input $(f,t_{n+1},h_n,r_n,Y_{n-1},Y_n,B_{n+1})$, it returns `evaluation-failure` if $f(t_{n+1},\cdot)$ is not defined throughout $B_{n+1}$. Otherwise it returns `no-root` if the equation has no root in that ball, `ambiguous-branch` if it has more than one, or $(\texttt{unique-root},Z)$ with the exact root if it has exactly one. Oracle calls are returning primitives; a realization of this procedure must supply an oracle meeting this contract for every call it reaches. This is an algorithm relative to that oracle; the vector field and ball alone do not provide a general exact root-counting or root-solving procedure.

For $n=1,\ldots,N-1$, form the equation and call $\mathcal O$ with the current history and prescribed ball:

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)Z-(1+r_n)^2Y_n+r_n^2Y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}=f(t_{n+1},Z).$$

On $(\texttt{unique-root},Z)$, set $Y_{n+1}=Z$ and continue. On any of the three failure statuses, return that status with the computed prefix. On reaching $N$, return `completed` and $(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)$. The procedure admits arbitrary positive adjacent step ratios; no convergence or accuracy property is part of this algorithm.

The coefficients are those obtained from the quadratic interpolation derivative in [[lem-variable-step-bdf2-interpolation-and-local-defect]]. A separate theorem gives the uniform ratio hypotheses needed for second-order convergence; they are not part of this algorithm.

Let $h_{n-1},h_n>0$, $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}$, and let $y$ be an exact solution with three continuous derivatives near $t_{n-1},t_n,t_{n+1}$, where $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$. The derivative at $t_{n+1}$ of the quadratic interpolant through $(t_{n+1},y_{n+1})$, $(t_n,y_n)$, and $(t_{n-1},y_{n-1})$ is

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)y_{n+1}-(1+r_n)^2y_n+r_n^2y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}.$$

Equating this derivative to $f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$ defines the variable-step BDF2 formula

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)Y_{n+1}-(1+r_n)^2Y_n+r_n^2Y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}=f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1}).$$

For an exact vector solution $y'=f(t,y)$ whose third derivative is bounded, the unscaled residual

$$\tau_n=(1+2r_n)y(t_{n+1})-(1+r_n)^2y(t_n)+r_n^2y(t_{n-1})-h_n(1+r_n)y'(t_{n+1})$$

has norm $\|\tau_n\|_\infty=O(h_n^3)$ uniformly whenever $r_n$ stays in a fixed compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$; the formula and remainder hold componentwise.

Let $T>0$, $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$, $h=T/N>0$, $p\in\mathbb R$ with $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. Real powers of the positive base $h$ are as in [[def-real-power]]. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

By [F4], setting the adjacent-step ratio to $1$ gives an unscaled residual of size $O(h^3)$; division by $2h$ yields $\|\tau_n\|_2\le C_\tau h^2$. This also follows by applying [F6] componentwise to the exact solution through degree two.

By [F3] and step 1.1, the numerical recurrence is $(3X_n-4X_{n-1}+X_{n-2})/(2h)=F(t_n,X_n)+\delta_n+r^d_n$, while the exact defect definition gives the same formula with $X$ replaced by $\bar x$ and an added $\tau_n$. Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

Fix a semi-explicit presentation $x'=f(t,x,z)$, $0=g(t,x,z)$ as in [[def-semi-explicit-index-one-dae-and-consistent-initial-data]] and a sufficiently differentiable consistent local solution. Differentiate the algebraic constraint along the differential equation, substituting $x'=f(t,x,z)$ and any previously obtained derivative relations at each stage. The **differentiation index in this convention** is the least positive integer $k$ for which the original constraint and its first $k$ differentiated equations locally determine $z$ and $z'$, with the equation for the highest derivative of $z$ having an invertible square Jacobian on a neighborhood of the solution. If no such finite $k$ exists, this local index is undefined. This convention counts through the first derivative of the algebraic variables and is local to the fixed presentation; it is not a universal index theory for arbitrary implicit systems.

If $g_z$ is invertible, one differentiation gives

$$
g_t+g_x f+g_z z'=0,
$$

which determines $z'$, so the index is one. If $g_z$ is singular, the index must be checked from the actual differentiated equations; no index-one conclusion follows from this definition alone.

derivations.claim: Here $f(t,x,z)=z$ and $g(t,x,z)=x$, so $g_z=0$ at every point. The regular index-one hypothesis $g_z$ invertible therefore fails.

Along any solution, differentiating $g(x(t),z(t))=x(t)=0$ and substituting $x'=z$ gives $z=0$. Differentiating this relation gives $z'=0$. The original constraint does not involve $z$; the first differentiated relation determines $z$, and the second determines its first derivative. By [F2] the differentiation index is two.

For every real $M$, the candidate $(x,z)=(0,M)$ has algebraic residual $g(0,M)=0$, while step 2.1 shows that a solution has $z=0$. Taking arbitrarily small $M\ne0$ rules out any finite constant $C$ for which $|z|\le C|g(x,z)|$ throughout a neighborhood of $(0,0)$.

The pair $(0,1)$ satisfies $g(0,1)=0$, but a solution would require $z(0)=0$ by step 2.1, so it is not a consistent initial pair for a solution. The pair $(1,0)$ has $g(1,0)=1\ne0$, so it fails even algebraic consistency.

The constant functions $x(t)=0,z(t)=0$ satisfy both equations, so the system has a solution with the consistent initial pair $(0,0)$. The three boundary calculations above concern only this fixed index-two system and imply no index-one numerical guarantee.

derivations.claim: Differentiating $q^\mathsf Tq=\ell^2$ once and using $q'=v$ gives $q^\mathsf Tv=0$, the tangency condition. Differentiating a second time gives $0=\|v\|_2^2+q^\mathsf Tv'=\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2-\lambda q^\mathsf Tq$. Using [A1], this equation solves uniquely for $\lambda=(\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2)/\ell^2$.

Differentiate $\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2-\lambda\ell^2=0$, the second-derivative constraint from step 1.1. Since $q'=v$ and $v'=-g_0e_2-\lambda q$, this gives $0=2v^\mathsf Tv'-g_0v_2-\lambda'\ell^2=-3g_0v_2-2\lambda q^\mathsf Tv-\lambda'\ell^2=-3g_0v_2-\lambda'\ell^2$, where the last equality uses the tangency condition in step 1.1. Since $\ell>0$, this determines $\lambda'=-3g_0v_2/\ell^2$ with nonzero coefficient $-\ell^2$ on the highest algebraic derivative.

The original constraint does not contain $\lambda$; its first derivative yields tangency but not $\lambda$, its second derivative determines $\lambda$, and its third derivative determines $\lambda'$. The prolonged equations are regular because the multiplier coefficients are $-\ell^2$ at each of these latter solves. Therefore the least differentiation count in [F2] is three.

For example, $q_0=(\ell,0)$, $v_0=(0,s)$, and $\lambda_0=s^2/\ell^2$ satisfy the position and tangency constraints, and the multiplier formula in step 1.1 gives $\lambda_0$. Thus this tuple satisfies the initial conditions exposed by the first two differentiations.
